summary: Known: Stroeker and de Weger (1999, Theorem 3) list every integral point of the plane cubic (39) and show there are no others, by linear forms in elliptic logarithms and LLL reduction. The proof is not elementary and has not been formalised. This node is that theorem stated over ℤ, word for word.

references.title: T. Yamada, Necessary conditions for binomial collisions, arXiv:2002.07043 (2020)
references.note: Theorem 1.1: if C(2N+δ, N−M) = C(2N+L, N−K) with δ ∈ {0,1}, 0 ≤ M < K < N/2 and M ≤ 0.735K, then L > N(1.3132 log²(2N) − 2.00271). The proof uses N ≥ 500000, taken from BBdW 2017. A preprint; no journal version was found on 2026-10-29.

references.title: A. Blokhuis, A. E. Brouwer, B. M. M. de Weger, Binomial collisions and near collisions, Integers 17 (2017) #A64
references.note: The search over n ≤ 10^6 that gives N ≥ 500000 for any unknown collision.

summary: Known, from a preprint: this node is the case L ≤ N of Yamada's Theorem 1.1. For N ≥ 500000 the bound N(1.3132 log²(2N) − 2.00271) is far above N, so the theorem rules out every collision in the node's range. The proof uses explicit prime-gap results, estimates for the largest prime factor of a product of consecutive integers, and an explicit Stirling formula. It has not been formalised, and the preprint has not been refereed as far as is known.

references.note: Theorem 2: the integral solutions of C(Y,2) = C(X,5) are the twenty points listed in this node. The curve has genus 2 and its Jacobian has rank 6; the proof combines Baker's method with a Mordell–Weil sieve (§13, details omitted, MAGMA programs published).

summary: Known: Bugeaud, Mignotte, Siksek, Stoll and Tengely (2008, Theorem 2) find every integral solution of Y(Y−1)/2 = X(X−1)(X−2)(X−3)(X−4)/120. This node is that theorem multiplied by 120. The proof uses linear forms in logarithms and a Mordell–Weil sieve, and has not been formalised.

references.title: J. Nagura, On the interval containing at least one prime number, Proc. Japan Acad. 28 (1952) 177–181
references.note: For every x ≥ 25 there is a prime p with x < p < 6x/5.

summary: Known: Nagura (1952) proved that for every x ≥ 25 the interval (x, 6x/5) contains a prime. The proof is an explicit Chebyshev-type estimate of the prime-counting function; Mathlib has Bertrand's postulate (the interval (x, 2x]) but not this refinement.
